slides.heading: The Science of Decision Fatigue
slides.body: Why your brain gets worse at choosing as the day goes on

slides.heading: What Is Decision Fatigue?
slides.body: Decision fatigue is the mental exhaustion that comes from making too many choices. Each decision we make depletes a limited pool of cognitive energy, leaving us worse at choosing as the day progresses.

slides.heading: The Judge Study
slides.body: A landmark 2011 Israeli study found that judges granted parole 65% of the time at the start of a session — but nearly 0% just before breaks. After food and rest, approval rates jumped back to 65%. The only variable was mental fatigue.

slides.heading: How Many Decisions Do We Make Daily?
slides.body: Research estimates adults make 35,000 decisions per day — from tiny ones like what to eat to major ones like career choices. Most are unconscious, but even low-stakes choices draw on the same cognitive reserves.

slides.heading: The Default to Impulsive Choices
slides.body: When decision fatigue sets in, the brain takes two shortcuts: it makes increasingly impulsive choices (the 'why not?' mentality) or it defaults to doing nothing at all, avoiding the decision entirely to conserve energy.

slides.heading: The Glucose Connection
slides.body: Early research linked decision fatigue to blood sugar — the brain burns glucose when making choices. While the glucose theory is now debated, rest and nutrition still clearly restore decision-making quality. Hunger genuinely impairs judgment.

slides.heading: High-Stakes Examples
slides.body: CEOs sign worse deals late in the day. Doctors prescribe more unnecessary antibiotics as their shift continues. Shoppers buy more unhealthy food after a long day of choices. Decision fatigue shapes outcomes across every domain.

slides.heading: Strategies to Combat It
slides.body: Schedule big decisions in the morning when cognitive resources are fresh. Use decision frameworks or checklists to reduce mental load. Eliminate trivial choices where possible — habits and routines are cognitive shortcuts that preserve energy.

slides.heading: The 'Uniform Effect'
slides.body: Steve Jobs wore the same outfit daily to eliminate one decision. Barack Obama did the same with suits. By reducing low-stakes choices, they preserved mental bandwidth for decisions that truly mattered. Simplification is a performance strategy.

slides.heading: Decide Less, Choose Better
slides.body: Decision fatigue is real and measurable. Guard your best mental hours for your most important choices, automate the trivial ones, and remember: rest isn't laziness — it's how you restore the brain's most valuable resource.
